body_markdown:
Wireless charging is becoming an increasingly important feature in modern vehicles, but designing a single system capable of supporting different smartphones and Qi charging profiles introduces significant engineering challenges.


At[the ECCE Europe 2026 conference and exhibition](https://www.ecce-europe.org/2026/) , in Valencia, Spain, indie presented a new approach to wireless power transfer for automotive applications. The paper, **“ *Resonant Converter Design of Wireless Power Transmitter Topology for Smartphones in Automotive Application* ”** , written by Prince Kumar, Piotr Strycharski, and Jack Whittaker, explores how a single-coil wireless charger can support **Basic Power Profile (BPP)** , **Extended Power Profile (EPP)** , and **Magnetic Power Profile (MPP)** while maintaining stable and efficient power transfer across different operating conditions.


## The challenge: One charger, multiple charging conditions


A smartphone wireless charger may appear simple from the outside, but the electrical environment changes considerably depending on the device placed on the charging surface.


Receiver coils vary in inductance, geometry, and magnetic coupling. Phone placement, protective cases, separation distance, mechanical tolerances, and foreign objects can further affect coupling between the transmitter and receiver. Poor coupling can shift the system’s resonant frequency, reduce power-transfer efficiency, or even prevent charging from starting.


The challenge becomes even greater when supporting multiple Qi profiles.


BPP and EPP typically operate between around **125** **kHz** , while MPP requires fixed, almost 3 times higher operating frequency of **360 kHz** . MPP also uses magnetic alignment to improve coupling between the transmitter and receiver coils.


A successful automotive charger therefore needs to **adapt** to substantially different electrical conditions while remaining within the constraints of the automotive environment.


## A simpler transmitter architecture


The paper presented proposes a cost-effective **four-switch architecture** , combining a two-switch boost stage with a two-switch half-bridge inverter. This contrasts with a conventional eight-switch buck-boost plus full-bridge implementation, reducing the number of switching devices required.


The architecture also uses a ground-referenced gate drive for selecting the transmitter resonant capacitance, eliminating the need for floating level shifters and drivers. The paper identifies this reduced silicon area and component count as advantages for overall system cost and high-volume automotive production.


Another important design consideration is **Zero Voltage Switching** **(ZVS)** . By maintaining the resonant tank in the appropriate inductive operating region, the system can achieve soft switching, reducing capacitive turn-on losses. This is particularly important for mitigating high-frequency EMI in automotive environments.


## Adapting to different[Qi profiles](https://www.indie.inc/applications/automotive/wireless-charging/)


Rather than relying on a single operating configuration, the proposed transmitter adjusts several parameters according to the receiver and operating conditions.


These include:


- **Boost converter output voltage,** which regulates the voltage delivered to the resonant inverter stage.
- **Resonant tank capacitance** , which allows the system to adapt its resonant behavior.
- **Switching frequency** , with approximately 128 kHz used for BPP/EPP and 360 kHz for MPP.
- **MPP-specific transmitter capacitance selection** , which accounts for differences in coil coupling.


This coordinated approach allows a single transmitter architecture to **accommodate** different receiver configurations and Qi operating modes.


## What the simulation demonstrated


The simulation focused on how[transmitter and receiver](https://www.indie.inc/in-cabin-ux/) **resonant capacitance** , **boost voltage** , and **coil coupling** influence system performance. A representative transmitter configuration used a 9 µH transmitter inductance and 2.7 nF compensation capacitance, with receiver capacitances of 174 nF and 710 nF evaluated.


One of the most important results concerned MPP operation at **360 kHz** .


With a receiver capacitance of **710 nF** , the simulations showed that:


- A transmitter capacitance of **65 nF** provides higher gain at coupling coefficients up to approximately **0.8** .
- At coupling factors above approximately **0.8** , increasing the transmitter capacitance to **100 nF** helps maintain the desired system gain and operating conditions.


*Figure 1. Variation of rectifier output voltage (Vrect) with respect to transmitter resonant capacitance (Ctx) at a fixed boost output voltage of 24V* .


The simulation therefore demonstrates why the transmitter resonant capacitance needs to adapt as coupling changes, particularly for magnetically aligned MPP receivers.


The resulting design parameters were **365 nF Ctx at 128 kHz for BPP and EPP** , **65 nF at 360 kHz for low-coupling MPP** , and **100 nF at 360 kHz for high-coupling MPP** .


## From simulation to indie’s Wireless Charger


The paper that was presented did not stop at simulation. The proposed architecture was implemented in hardware using[indie’s iND87204 wireless charger IC](https://www.indie.inc/product/ind87204/) .


Experimental testing demonstrated operation with BPP, EPP, and MPP receivers at their respective operating frequencies, as well as ZVS operation across these receiver types. The iND87204 also supports programmable inverter dead time, allowing it to be dynamically adjusted according to the receiver to maintain sufficient ZVS without unnecessarily long dead-time intervals.


*Figure 2. Proposed transmitter topology* .


With the transmitter and receiver coils aligned, the paper reports measured end-to-end efficiencies ranging from **70% to 83%** across the tested phones. The highest reported values were **83%** for an **MPP iPhone 15 Pro** and **82%** for an **MPP iPhone 17 Pro** .


## Toward more flexible automotive wireless charging


The results presented showed that supporting multiple Qi profiles does not necessarily require completely different transmitter architectures. By coordinating **boost voltage** , **switching frequency** , and **resonant capacitance** , the proposed solution can adapt to different receiver types, operating frequencies, coupling conditions, and alignment scenarios.


The research demonstrates how a streamlined single-coil design can support BPP, EPP, and MPP within one solution, leveraging the[iND87204](https://www.indie.inc/product/ind87204/) wireless charger IC and an architecture developed specifically for automotive requirements.


By adapting to different receiver types, coupling conditions, and Qi operating profiles, the solution provides a flexible approach to reliable and efficient[in-vehicle wireless charging](https://www.indie.inc/applications/automotive/wireless-charging/) , while addressing key considerations such as system cost, EMI, and MPP magnetic alignment.


Note: This paper was presented at *[The ECCE Europe 2026 conference and exhibition](https://www.ecce-europe.org/2026/)* at the Valencia Conference Center in Valencia, Spain. ****
